transcript.text:
The first thing that sorts this out is whether it's completely dead or whether it has power but won't start a cycle. Here are the likely causes, roughly most likely first: - No power reaching it: the plug, the socket, or the switched spur. That's often a separate switch above the worktop or in a nearby cupboard. It could also be the fuse in the plug.
• The door not being detected as shut: something in the racks stopping the door closing fully, or a worn door latch or switch. In that case the lights usually come on but it won't run.
• A setting: a child or control lock that stops the buttons responding, or a delay start that makes it look as if nothing's happening.
• Less often, a fault in the mains input or the control board. That's more likely if it's totally dead even though the power is fine. Safe checks to try: 1. Power. Make sure the plug is fully in and the socket and any spur switch are on. Then plug something else, like a kettle, into the same socket. - If the other appliance doesn't work, it's the supply, not the dishwasher. - If a circuit breaker or RCD has tripped, reset it once only. If it trips again, leave it off, because that points to a fault.
2. Door. Open it and check no plate, tall item, rack or cutlery basket is sticking out. Shut it firmly until it clicks, then choose a programme and press start. - If it now starts, something was stopping the door closing. - If it has lights but still acts as if the door is open, the latch or door switch is the suspect.
3. Lock or delay. Look for a key or padlock symbol, or a countdown such as "3h", on the display. - A lock symbol means the child lock is on. Your manual shows which buttons to hold to turn it off. - A countdown means a delay start is set. Cancel it and try again. When you press the power button, does anything light up at all, or is it completely dead? That tells us whether to look at the power and electrics or at the door and settings.
completely dead, nothing lights up at all. other sockets and lights in the kitchen work fine though

Completely dead with no lights at all points to power not getting into the machine, or a fault right at its electrical front end. Other kitchen sockets working is a good sign, but dishwashers are often on their own circuit: a socket hidden behind the unit, or a switched fused spur with its own fuse. So the supply isn't ruled out yet. Most likely causes, in order:
1. No power at the dishwasher itself. This could be its own socket, the spur switch, the fuse in the spur, or the fuse in its plug.
2. The door not being detected as latched. Some machines stay completely blank until the door is properly shut.
3. A fault inside: the mains input, the on/off switch or the control board. Checks to separate these:
1. Check its own supply. Find the dishwasher's actual socket or spur. Make sure the spur switch is on, then plug a kettle or lamp into that same socket if you can reach it. - Nothing works there: it's the supply, not the dishwasher. - It works: the supply is fine, so move on. - If you find a fused spur with no socket, its fuse may have blown. An electrician can check it, or you can swap it yourself if you're confident, with the spur switched off.
2. Try a new plug fuse. Switch off and unplug, then fit a known-good 13A fuse in the dishwasher's plug. You can borrow one from another appliance's plug to test. - If it comes back to life, it was just the fuse. - If it blows again straight away, stop. That points to an internal fault.
3. Check the door. Shut it firmly until it clicks, then press the power button again. - If it lights up now, the door latch wasn't engaging. - If it lights up only when you push on the door, the latch or door switch is suspect. If the socket is proven live, the fuse is good and it's still dead with the door latched, the fault is most likely inside the machine: the door switch, the mains input or the control board. That's usually a job for an engineer, because it means taking panels off and testing the wiring.

spur switch above the worktop is on and the neon light is lit. door's shut and latched firmly. nothing tripped at the consumer unit. I don't know how to check the fuse in the spur and I've no spare fuse or meter

Checking the spur fuse is simpler than it sounds. Most fused spurs have a small fuse holder on the front faceplate, usually a little slotted cover marked "FUSE" or with a fuse symbol. 1. Switch the spur off.
2. Prise the holder out gently with a small flat screwdriver in the slot. It should pop out with the fuse sitting in it.
3. Check the rating printed on the fuse, normally 13A. That said, the neon light helps here. On most fused spurs the neon is wired after the fuse, so if it's lit the spur fuse is usually fine. That isn't guaranteed on every type, but it makes the spur less likely to be the problem. That leaves two main possibilities: 1. A blown fuse further along. If the spur feeds a socket that the dishwasher plugs into, the 13A fuse in the dishwasher's own plug may have gone. This is the most common, cheapest cause of a totally dead machine.
2. A fault inside the machine. This could be the on/off switch, the mains input/filter or the control board. Less often it's the door switch, as some dishwashers stay completely blank until they detect the door is shut, and yours is latching properly. You don't need a meter to rule out the fuse. A card of 13A plug fuses costs a pound or two from a supermarket or hardware shop. Switch off, unplug, swap the fuse in the dishwasher's plug and try again.
• If it comes back to life, it was just the fuse.
• If it blows again or trips something, stop using it. That points to an internal fault. If there's no plug and the cable goes straight into the spur, or a fresh fuse makes no difference, the power is probably reaching the machine and the fault is inside it. Finding it means taking panels off and testing the wiring, so that's a job for an engineer. On an older, cheaper machine it's worth asking for a rough quote first, as a control board can cost a fair bit compared with a new dishwasher. So, does your dishwasher plug into a socket somewhere near it, or is its cable wired straight into the spur?
not sure, I can't pull the dishwasher out to see. it's an integrated one. what should I do next?

That's fine, you don't need to pull it out. A lit neon on the spur means power is very likely reaching the dishwasher's circuit. So it comes down to two things: a blown fuse in the dishwasher's own plug, if it has one, or a fault inside the machine (the on/off switch, mains input or control board). Here's what to try next, easiest first. 1. Do a power reset. Switch the spur off, wait a full 5 minutes, then switch it back on. Shut the door and press power. Control boards sometimes lock up and need this to wake.
• If it comes on, it was a glitch. Keep an eye on it. If it keeps happening, that points to the control board. 2. Look for its plug without moving the machine. On integrated dishwashers the socket is very often in the cupboard next to it, usually under the sink at the back. If not, it may be behind the plinth (the kick panel under the doors). Most plinths unclip or pull off from the front.
• Switch the spur off first and use a torch.
• If you find a plug, pick up a card of 13A fuses from a supermarket or hardware shop. Swap the fuse in the plug, then switch back on and try it.
• If it comes back to life, that was the fault. If the new fuse blows, stop using it, because that means something inside is shorting. 3. If you can't find a plug, or a new fuse makes no difference, it's most likely an internal fault. Finding it means testing the wiring inside, so that's an engineer's job. It also usually means sliding the machine out, which they'll do for you. Ask for a rough quote first. If it turns out to be the control board on an older machine, compare the cost against a new dishwasher before going ahead. Let me know how the reset goes and whether you spot a socket.
ok, I'll try the 5 minute reset on the spur. will report back

Sounds good. While you're doing it, a couple of things to watch for. 1. Give it the full 5 minutes off. Control boards hold a little charge and need time to fully reset.
2. When you switch back on, shut the door firmly, then press and hold the power button for a second or two.
3. Listen as well as look. A faint click, a beep or a brief hum when you switch the spur back on means power is getting in, which points more towards the control side than the fuse. What the result means:
• If it lights up, it was most likely a board lock-up. If it happens again, that points to the control board.
• If it's still completely silent and dark, the next step is the plug fuse, if you can find a plug in the next cupboard or behind the plinth. If you can't find one, it's an engineer's job to test the power input and board. Let me know what happens.
ok, done the 5 minutes and switched it back on. still completely dead, no lights, no click or beep. what now?

No click, beep or light even after a full reset means power is very likely not getting into the electronics at all. With the spur on and its neon lit, that leaves two realistic explanations: 1. A blown fuse in the dishwasher's own plug. This only applies if it plugs into a socket rather than being wired straight into the spur. It's cheap and quick to rule out, so it's worth one last look.
2. A fault inside the machine. This is the more likely of the two if there's no plug. The usual suspects are the on/off switch, the mains input/interference filter, or the power supply on the control board. Less often it's the door switch or the wiring that runs through the door hinge, as some machines stay totally blank without it. What to do now: 1. Have one quick look for a socket without moving anything. Switch the spur off, open the cupboard under the sink or the one beside the dishwasher, and shine a torch at the back. If you find a plug, fit a new 13A fuse, then switch back on and try it. • If it comes on, that was the fault. • If the new fuse blows, stop using it, because something inside is shorting.
2. If there's no plug to be found, or a new fuse changes nothing, stop there. Finding which internal part has failed means sliding the machine out, taking panels off and testing with power applied. That's an engineer's job, and they'll handle moving it. On whether it's worth repairing: if it turns out to be a switch, the mains filter or a door wire, it's usually a sensible repair. A control board is the expensive one. On a machine more than about 8 to 10 years old, or a budget model, a new dishwasher can make more sense, so ask the engineer for a quote once they've diagnosed it. If you tell me the make and roughly how old it is, I can say more about whether a repair is likely to be worth it. I can also tell you whether it's worth checking for any safety recall.
